board_events.text: Integration: undoing the derivative
Differentiation gives a rate of change. Integration reverses it: from the rate, rebuild the function.
If $F'(x)=f(x)$, then $F(x)$ is an anti-derivative of $f(x)$.
Differentiation erases constants, so we can't recover which one — we add $+C$.
The answer is never one curve but a whole family $F(x)+C$, stacked vertically.

board_events.text: Along a line $x=a$, every curve has slope $f(a)$ — shifting up or down never changes steepness.
Standard forms and the two workhorse rules

board_events.latex: \int e^x\,dx = e^x + C \qquad \int a^x\,dx = \frac{a^x}{\ln a} + C
\int \cos x\,dx = \sin x + C \qquad \int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x + C
\int \sec^2 x\,dx = \tan x + C \qquad \int \csc^2 x\,dx = -\cot x + C

board_events.text: Linearity: $\int[k_1 f + k_2 g]\,dx = k_1\int f\,dx + k_2\int g\,dx$ — sums and constants only.
Self-check any row by differentiating the right side; if you don't get the integrand back, it's wrong.
Example 1: split with linearity
Evaluate $\int\left(3x^2+\tfrac{4}{x}-5\sec^2 x\right)dx$.
Split term by term, pull out constants, then use rows one, two and seven.
Example 2: divide before you integrate
Evaluate $\int \frac{x^2+2x+5}{x}\,dx$ — the trap is reaching for a substitution.
Split the fraction first: $\frac{x^2+2x+5}{x} = x + 2 + \frac{5}{x}$.
Polynomial over a single monomial? Divide through first — save a minute, skip the substitution.
Example 3: an identity clears the way
Evaluate $\int \frac{\cos 2x}{\cos^2 x\,\sin^2 x}\,dx$.
Use $\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x$, then split over the denominator.

board_events.latex: \frac{\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x\,\sin^2 x} = \frac{1}{\sin^2 x} - \frac{1}{\cos^2 x} = \csc^2 x - \sec^2 x

board_events.text: Example 4: recover a function from its slope
Given $f'(x)=\frac{(x+1)(x-1)}{x}$ for $x>0$, through $(1,\tfrac{3}{2})$. Simplify: $f'(x)=x-\tfrac{1}{x}$.
The point pins $C$: $\tfrac{3}{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} + C \Rightarrow C = 1$, so $f(x)=\tfrac{x^2}{2}-\ln x + 1$ and $f(e)=\tfrac{e^2}{2}$.
A boundary condition turns the whole family into one function — the bridge to differential equations.
The five slips that cost easy marks
Forgetting $+C$ is the most-penalised Board error. Write it the instant you finish.
Never apply the power rule at $n=-1$: $\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x|+C$, a separate memorised result — not $\frac{x^0}{0}$.
Keep the modulus in $\ln|x|$: the integrand $\frac{1}{x}$ is defined for negative $x$ too, so it's required, not decoration.
Sign trap: $\int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x$ but $\int \cos x\,dx = +\sin x$. The minus lives with sine.
Linearity covers sums and constant multiples only — never $\int(f\cdot g)=\int f\cdot\int g$. Products and quotients need their own methods.
The universal safety net: differentiate your answer. Integration is the one operation you can instantly self-check.

segments.text: <curious>Let me start with a question that turns everything you know about derivatives around.
Differentiation takes a function and hands you its rate of change. Integration asks the reverse, harder question: given the rate at every instant, can I rebuild the original function?
We name that rebuilt function. If capital F differentiates to little f, then capital F is an anti-derivative of f — it literally un-does the derivative.

Now the crucial catch. When you differentiate, every constant vanishes: x squared plus seven and x squared minus a hundred have the same derivative. Running it backwards, you can't tell which constant was there, so we honestly write plus C.
So the integral of two x is x squared plus C, where C is any constant at all.
That means an indefinite integral is never a single curve. It's an entire family, F of x, F of x plus one, F of x plus two, stacked like a ladder.
Picture that ladder: identical curves, each lifted by its own value of C.

<chuckle>And here's the pretty part. Pick any vertical line x equals a. It cuts every curve, and the tangent at each crossing has the same slope, because sliding a curve up or down never changes how steep it is.
Here's the toolkit you must know cold. Every direct integral in this subtopic is just pattern-matching to one of these rows.
The power rule: x to the n integrates to x to the n plus one, over n plus one, valid for every n except minus one, where the denominator would blow up.
That single exception, one over x, integrates to log of the absolute value of x. Keep the modulus, since one over x is defined for negative x too.
Exponentials: e to the x integrates to itself; a general base a to the x picks up a division by natural log a.
The trig pair to burn in: cosine integrates to plus sine, but sine integrates to minus cosine. The minus lives with the sine integral.
Secant squared gives tangent; cosecant squared gives minus cotangent, these are just the derivative table read backwards.
And two inverse-trig forms: one over one plus x squared gives arctan x; one over root one minus x squared gives arcsin x.
Tying it together is linearity: you may split sums and pull out constant multiples freely. But never products or quotients, those need real methods later.
One habit makes the whole table self-verifying: differentiate your answer. If it doesn't return the integrand, hunt for the slip.
Let's put the table to work. First a clean Board-level split.
We want the integral of three x squared, plus four over x, minus five secant squared x.
Linearity lets us break this into three separate integrals and pull the constants out front, then match rows one, two, and seven of the table.
Row one turns three x squared into x cubed; four over x becomes four log mod x; five secant squared becomes five tan x. Notice the single C at the end, and the modulus inside the log.
<curious>Now a J E E speed trap, where the obvious move is the wrong one.
We want the integral of x squared plus two x plus five, all over x. The trap is reaching for a substitution.
Don't. Just split the fraction term by term: it becomes x plus two plus five over x.
Now every piece is a standard form: x squared over two, plus two x, plus five log mod x, plus C.
The lesson: whenever a polynomial sits over a single monomial, divide through first. You'll save time and dodge a needless substitution.
This one looks brutal until an identity dissolves it.
We want the integral of cosine two x, over cosine squared x times sine squared x.
Rewrite cosine two x as cosine squared minus sine squared, then split that over the denominator.
The cosine squared over cosine squared sine squared collapses to one over sine squared; the other term to one over cosine squared. Those are cosecant squared minus secant squared.
And those integrate straight from the table: minus cotangent x, minus tangent x, plus C. The whole difficulty was algebraic.
<curious>Now an Advanced problem that hides integration inside a slope question.
We're given f prime of x, and told the graph passes through the point one, three-halves. First simplify the derivative to x minus one over x.
Integrate to get the family: x squared over two, minus log x, plus C.

The passing-through point fixes C. Plug in: three-halves equals one-half plus C, so C is one. That selects one curve, f of x is x squared over two minus log x plus one, and f of e is e squared over two.
The deep idea: a single boundary condition converts an entire family into one unique function. That's exactly the bridge to differential equations later this year.
Let's lock in the mistakes that quietly bleed marks, because avoiding them is free points.
Number one: forgetting plus C. In Boards it's the most penalised error, a perfect function part still loses marks without it. Train the reflex to write plus C the instant you finish.
Number two: never apply the power rule at n equals minus one. One over x does not become x to the zero over zero. It's a separate, memorised result, log mod x plus C.
Number three: keep the modulus in log mod x. Since one over x is defined for negative x as well, the absolute value is mathematically required, not decoration.
Number four, the classic sign slip: sine integrates to minus cosine, but cosine integrates to plus sine. The minus lives with the sine integral.
Number five: linearity is only for sums and constant multiples. The integral of a product is not the product of integrals, those need their own methods.
<whisper>Here's the secret weapon on the board: differentiate what you wrote, and check it equals the integrand.
Do that every time. Integration is the only school-level operation you can instantly reverse-check, and if the derivative isn't the integrand, you've caught your mistake before the examiner did.

board_events.text: Substitution: the chain rule in reverse
The table can't touch $\int 2x\cos(x^2)\,dx$ — there's no entry for $\cos(x^2)$.
Chain rule: $\frac{d}{dx}F(g(x)) = F'(g(x))\,g'(x)$. So (function of $g$)$\times g'$ is a disguised derivative.
The step $du = g'(x)\,dx$ is the exchange rate — forget it and the answer is wrong.

board_events.text: Substitution only helps when $g'(x)$ — or a constant times it — is actually present.
For an indefinite integral, always convert back to $x$ at the end.
The two patterns and four results to know
In words: a numerator that is the derivative of the denominator integrates to log of the denominator.

board_events.latex: \int \tan x\,dx = \ln|\sec x| + C \qquad \int \cot x\,dx = \ln|\sin x| + C
\int \sec x\,dx = \ln|\sec x + \tan x| + C \qquad \int \csc x\,dx = \ln|\csc x - \cot x| + C

board_events.text: The $\tan$ and $\sec$ results are the $\int f'/f$ pattern in disguise — numerator equals the denominator's derivative.
Reflex: is the numerator a constant times the derivative of the denominator? If yes, the answer is a log.
Example 1: the derivative is already there
Evaluate $\int 2x\sqrt{x^2+1}\,dx$. Let $u=x^2+1$, so $du=2x\,dx$.
Example 2: spot f-prime over f instantly
Evaluate $\int \frac{x}{x^2+4}\,dx$. Derivative of $x^2+4$ is $2x$, and $x=\tfrac{1}{2}(2x)$.
Numerator a constant times the denominator's derivative? Write (constant) times ln(denominator) at once.
Example 3: a nested substitution
Evaluate $\int \frac{e^{\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$. Let $u=\sqrt{x}$, so $\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}}=2\,du$.
Example 4: substitute the root away
Evaluate $\int \frac{1}{1+\sqrt{x}}\,dx$. Put $x=t^2$ ($t\ge 0$): $dx=2t\,dt$, $\sqrt{x}=t$.
The split $\frac{t}{1+t}=1-\frac{1}{1+t}$ (an improper fraction) is a recurring trick — keep it handy.
Where substitution quietly goes wrong
Replace $g'(x)\,dx$ with $du$ — not just $g(x)$ with $u$. Dropping the $du$ is the number-one error.
For an indefinite integral, always back-substitute to $x$. Leaving the answer in $u$ loses marks.
Mind the constant factor in $f'/f$: $\int\frac{x}{x^2+a^2}$ carries a $\tfrac{1}{2}$; $\int\frac{2x}{x^2+a^2}$ does not.
Sign check: $\int\tan x = +\ln|\sec x|$ and $\int\cot x = +\ln|\sin x|$.
Substitution only works if $g'$ is present. If it isn't, don't force it — reach for a different method.
The reflex handling a huge share of exam integrals: check if the numerator is the derivative of the denominator first.

segments.text: <curious>What do you do when the integrand simply isn't in the table?
Take the integral of two x times cosine of x squared. There's no row for cosine of x squared, so we're stuck, until we reshape it.

The idea mirrors the chain rule in reverse. The chain rule says the derivative of F of g of x is F prime of g, times g prime of x. So if an integrand looks like a function of g, times g prime, it's exactly a disguised derivative.
So we peel off the inner function, call it u, and the whole thing becomes the integral of f of u, du, clean and familiar.
The one step everyone forgets is the accounting: d u equals g prime of x d x. Think of it as the exchange rate, drop it and your answer is off by a factor.
Picture converting rupees to another currency: switch to the u-world, do the easy shopping, then convert your answer back to the x-world.
Substitution only helps when g prime of x, or a constant multiple of it, is actually sitting in the integrand. If it's missing, this method stalls.
And for an indefinite integral, always convert back to x at the very end, never leave your answer in u.
Substitution has two master patterns; memorise these and half of exam integrals fall instantly.
First, the logarithmic pattern: the integral of f prime over f is log of the absolute value of f.
Say it in words, whenever the numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator, the answer is log of that denominator. This one reflex is worth a lot of marks.
Second, the power-chain pattern: a function to the n, times its own derivative, integrates like the power rule, f to the n plus one, over n plus one.
From these we derive four standard results. Tan x integrates to log mod sec x; cot x to log mod sin x.
And the trickier pair: sec x integrates to log mod sec x plus tan x; cosec x to log mod cosec x minus cot x.
Both the tan and sec results are secretly the f prime over f pattern, in each case the numerator turns out to be the derivative of the denominator.
So train one question before you compute: is the numerator a constant times the derivative of the denominator? If yes, write log immediately, no formal substitution needed.
Let's spot inner functions in the wild. First, one where the derivative is handed to us.
We want the integral of two x times root x squared plus one. Let u be x squared plus one; then d u is exactly two x d x, and that two x d x is sitting right there.
So the integral becomes root u d u, which is u to the three-halves, over three-halves, that is, two-thirds u to the three-halves.
Back-substitute u equals x squared plus one, and we're done: two-thirds times x squared plus one, to the three-halves, plus C.
<excited>Now watch how the f prime over f reflex skips the busywork entirely.
We want the integral of x over x squared plus four. The derivative of the denominator is two x, and our numerator x is just half of that.
So pull out the one-half: the integral becomes one-half log of x squared plus four, plus C, no formal u needed.
That's the shortcut: whenever the numerator is a constant times the denominator's derivative, write constant times log of the denominator immediately.
This one nests a root inside an exponent, perfect for a clean substitution.
We want the integral of e to the root x, over root x. Let u be root x; then d u is one over two root x d x, which means d x over root x equals two d u.
Rewrite the integral: e to the root x times d x over root x becomes e to the u times two d u, which is just two e to the u, plus C.
Back-substitute u equals root x: the answer is two e to the root x, plus C. The awkward one over root x was exactly twice the derivative of the exponent.
<curious>Now what if the root blocks every table entry? Substitute it away entirely.
We want the integral of one over one plus root x. Put x equals t squared, so d x is two t d t and root x is just t.
The integral becomes two t over one plus t d t. Split that improper fraction as one minus one over one plus t, and integrate: two times t minus log mod one plus t.
Back-substitute t equals root x: two root x minus two log of one plus root x, plus C.
Tuck away that move, splitting t over one plus t into one minus one over one plus t. That improper-fraction split shows up again and again.
A few small habits separate a clean substitution from a wrong one. Let's name them.
First and biggest: you must replace g prime of x d x with d u, not just swap g of x for u. Dropping the d u accounting is the single most common substitution error.
Second: for an indefinite integral, always convert back to x. An answer left in u is incomplete and loses marks.

Third, the constant factor. The integral of x over x squared plus a squared carries a one-half; but two x over x squared plus a squared does not. Check whether your numerator is the whole derivative or a fraction of it.
Fourth, a sign check: tan x integrates to plus log mod sec x, and cot x to plus log mod sin x. Get the signs from the derivation, not from guessing.
And remember, substitution only works if g prime is actually present. If it isn't, don't force the method, step back and pick another.
The board sums up the golden reflex: if the numerator is a constant times the derivative of the denominator, the answer is a log.
<whisper>Ask that one question before you write anything, and a huge share of exam integrals become one-liners.

board_events.text: The templates to recognise
Sign in the denominator picks the function: $+\to\tan^{-1}$, $-\to$ log-of-ratio. And $\sin^{-1}$ carries no $\tfrac{1}{a}$.
For $px+q$ over a quadratic: write $px+q = \lambda\,\tfrac{d}{dx}(\text{quad}) + \mu$; the $\lambda$-part gives log or root, the $\mu$-part a template.
Example 1: a direct arctan
Evaluate $\int \frac{dx}{x^2+9}$. Match $\int\frac{dx}{x^2+a^2}$ with $a=3$.
Example 2: a direct log ratio
Evaluate $\int \frac{dx}{x^2-16}$. Match $\int\frac{dx}{x^2-a^2}$ with $a=4$, so $\tfrac{1}{2a}=\tfrac{1}{8}$.
Read the sign first: $x^2+a^2$ gives arctan; $x^2-a^2$ gives a log of a ratio.
Same-looking denominators, opposite answers — the plus/minus decides everything.
Example 3: complete the square
Evaluate $\int \frac{dx}{x^2+4x+13}$. Complete the square: $x^2+4x+13=(x+2)^2+9$.
Example 4: a linear numerator over a root
Evaluate $\int \frac{2x+3}{\sqrt{x^2+4x+8}}\,dx$. Since $\tfrac{d}{dx}(x^2+4x+8)=2x+4$, write $2x+3=(2x+4)-1$.
Leftover: $x^2+4x+8=(x+2)^2+4$, so $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x+2)^2+4}}=\ln\left|(x+2)+\sqrt{x^2+4x+8}\right|$.
Split a linear numerator into (derivative-part) + (constant-part) — the master key for (linear)/(quadratic).
Three binary checks pin the template
$x^2+a^2$ (arctan) vs $x^2-a^2$ (log): the denominator's sign picks the function. Read it first.
The $\tfrac{1}{a}$ factor: $\int\frac{dx}{x^2+a^2}$ has it; $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}=\sin^{-1}\tfrac{x}{a}$ has none.
Numerator $x$ vs $1$: numerator $x$ goes to a log via $f'/f$; a constant numerator goes to arctan or arcsin.
Any $x^2+bx+c$ must be reshaped by completing the square before a template applies.
Check one — sign: log or arctan? Check two — root present: arcsin or log-root? Check three — numerator $x$ or $1$?
Three binary checks pin the template before you write a single symbol.
Partial fractions: addition run in reverse
Some rationals like $\frac{1}{(x-1)(x+2)}$ have no direct integral — no single substitution simplifies them.
Break one complicated fraction into a sum of simpler ones, each integrating to a log or arctan.

The denominator must be factorised; each factor type gets its own partial-fraction template.
It's literally the addition of fractions, run backwards to recover the unknown numerators.

segments.text: These are the templates to burn into memory. Every problem in this subtopic is completing the square, then matching one of these.
First: one over x squared plus a squared integrates to one over a, arctan x over a. The plus sign gives you arctan.
Change that plus to a minus: one over x squared minus a squared integrates to one over two a, log of the ratio x minus a over x plus a.
Under a root: one over root a squared minus x squared is arcsine x over a, and notice, no one-over-a factor out front.
The other two root forms both give a log: one over root x squared plus or minus a squared integrates to log of x plus that same root.
Then the square-root integrals themselves. Root a squared minus x squared integrates to x over two times the root, plus a squared over two times arcsine x over a.
And root x squared plus a squared integrates to x over two times the root, plus a squared over two times the log form. There's a matching result for x squared minus a squared.
The single most important reading: the sign in the denominator picks the function, plus gives arctan, minus gives a log ratio. And remember the arcsine form carries no one-over-a.
Finally, for a linear numerator p x plus q over a quadratic, write it as lambda times the derivative of the quadratic, plus mu. The lambda part gives a log or a root; the mu part is a pure template.
Two lookups first, to lock in reading the sign.
We want the integral of one over x squared plus nine. Match the arctan template with a equals three.
So the answer is one-third arctan x over three, plus C. Clean.
Now change one symbol, a minus instead of a plus.
We want one over x squared minus sixteen. Match the log template with a equals four, so one over two a is one-eighth.
The answer is one-eighth log of the ratio x minus four over x plus four, plus C.
The whole game is reading the sign first. A plus in the denominator gives arctan; a minus gives a log of a ratio.
Two denominators that look almost identical produce completely different answers, the plus or minus decides everything, so read it before you write.
Now the real skill: reshaping before matching.
We want one over x squared plus four x plus thirteen. Complete the square: that denominator is x plus two, all squared, plus nine.
With capital X equal to x plus two, it's the arctan template with a equals three, one-third arctan X over three.
Convert back: the answer is one-third arctan of x plus two over three, plus C.
<curious>Now the boss level, a linear numerator sitting over the root of a quadratic.
We want two x plus three, over root x squared plus four x plus eight. The derivative of the inside is two x plus four, so write two x plus three as two x plus four, minus one.
The two x plus four part is exactly the derivative of the inside, so it integrates by the f prime over root f rule to two times the root.
The leftover minus one part: complete the square to x plus two squared plus four, and it becomes log of x plus two, plus the root.
Combine: two times the root, minus log of x plus two plus the root, plus C.
Bank this move, splitting a linear numerator into a derivative part plus a constant part. It's the master key for every linear-over-quadratic integral, root or no root.
This subtopic rewards a quick triage. Three yes-or-no checks decide the whole answer.
Check the denominator's sign first. x squared plus a squared gives arctan; x squared minus a squared gives a log of a ratio. Same-looking forms, opposite answers.
Watch the one-over-a factor. The arctan template carries a one-over-a out front, but the arcsine template, one over root a squared minus x squared, carries none. Mixing these up is a classic slip.
Look at the numerator. If it's an x, you're heading to a log through the f prime over f pattern. If it's a constant, you're heading to arctan or arcsine. Same denominator, different problems.
And never forget to complete the square. Any x squared plus b x plus c has to be reshaped before any template applies.
So run three checks. One: the sign, log or arctan? Two: is there a root, arcsine or log-root? Three: numerator x or one?
The board shows the chain: sign, then root, then numerator.
<whisper>Those three binary checks pin the exact template before you write a single symbol.
<curious>What do you do with a fraction that no substitution will simplify?
Take one over x minus one, times x plus two. There's no single substitution that cracks it, and it's not in any table.
The fix is to break that one complicated fraction into a sum of simpler fractions, each of which integrates cleanly to a log or an arctan.
So we claim it equals A over x minus one, plus B over x plus two, for some constants A and B we'll find.

sections.title: Templates and the cover-up shortcut & related topics

board_events.text: One term per factor
Each term then integrates: linear to a log, repeated to a power, quadratic to a log plus an arctan.
Cover-up (distinct linear): to find the numerator over $(x-r)$, delete that factor and set $x=r$.
Solve constants by substituting roots (fast) or by comparing coefficients (for repeated/quadratic).
Example 1: two distinct linear factors
Evaluate $\int \frac{dx}{(x-1)(x+2)}$. Cover-up: $A=\tfrac{1}{3}$ at $x=1$, $B=-\tfrac{1}{3}$ at $x=-2$.
Example 2: cover-up with a linear numerator
Evaluate $\int \frac{3x+1}{(x+1)(x-2)}\,dx$. Over $(x+1)$, $x=-1\to\tfrac{2}{3}$; over $(x-2)$, $x=2\to\tfrac{7}{3}$.
Cover-up finds each constant in one substitution — no system of equations.
Example 3: a repeated linear factor
Evaluate $\int \frac{x}{(x-1)^2(x+1)}\,dx$. Template: $\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{(x-1)^2}+\frac{C}{x+1}$.
Clear denominators; $x=1\Rightarrow B=\tfrac{1}{2}$; $x=-1\Rightarrow C=-\tfrac{1}{4}$; compare $x^2\Rightarrow A=\tfrac{1}{4}$.
Example 4: an improper fraction
Evaluate $\int \frac{x^3}{x^2+1}\,dx$. Degree $3\ge 2$ — divide first: $\frac{x^3}{x^2+1}=x-\frac{x}{x^2+1}$.
The second piece is an $f'/f$ form — numerator $x$ is half the derivative of $x^2+1$.
Always test degree first — skipping division on an improper fraction is the top way this goes wrong.
Partial-fraction traps
Numerator degree $\ge$ denominator degree? Divide first. Forcing partial fractions on an improper fraction gives wrong constants.
A repeated factor $(x-a)^2$ needs both $\frac{A}{x-a}$ and $\frac{B}{(x-a)^2}$ — not just one.
An irreducible quadratic takes a linear numerator $Ax+B$; a linear factor takes a constant $A$.
Combining logs: $\ln|a|-\ln|b|=\ln|a/b|$ — track which factor is on top.
For distinct linear factors, skip the linear system — use cover-up, one substitution per constant.
Reserve coefficient-comparison for repeated or quadratic factors, where cover-up alone can't finish.
Integration by parts: the product rule reversed
Substitution needs a function times its own derivative. But what about $x\cos x$ or $xe^x$?
Parts is built for products of two unrelated functions — the reverse of the product rule.

segments.text: The decomposition follows one rule: one partial fraction per factor, matched to the factor's type.
A plain linear factor a x plus b gets a single constant over it, A over a x plus b.
A repeated linear factor, a x plus b squared, needs two terms: A over the factor, plus B over the factor squared.
An irreducible quadratic factor takes a linear numerator on top: A x plus B, over that quadratic.
Once split, each term integrates predictably: a linear factor gives a log, a repeated factor gives a power, and a quadratic gives a log plus an arctan.
Note the repeated case explicitly: one over x minus a, squared, integrates to minus one over x minus a, a power, not a log.
For distinct linear factors, the fastest trick is cover-up: to get the numerator over x minus r, delete that factor from the original and set x equal to r.
In general, find the constants either by substituting the roots, quick, or by comparing coefficients, which you'll need for repeated or quadratic factors.
Let's see the cover-up shortcut in action on two distinct linear factors.
We want one over x minus one, times x plus two. By cover-up: delete x minus one and set x to one, giving A equals one-third; delete x plus two and set x to minus two, giving B equals minus one-third.
So the fraction splits as one-third over x minus one, minus one-third over x plus two.
Each piece is a log, and combining them gives one-third log of the ratio x minus one over x plus two, plus C.
<excited>The same trick handles a linear numerator too, just as fast.
We want three x plus one, over x plus one times x minus two. Cover-up over x plus one: set x to minus one, and the rest gives two-thirds. Over x minus two: set x to two, giving seven-thirds.
So the integral is two-thirds log mod x plus one, plus seven-thirds log mod x minus two, plus C.
The payoff: cover-up finds each constant in a single substitution, with no system of equations to solve.
Now a repeated factor, where the template grows an extra term.
We want x over x minus one squared, times x plus one. Because x minus one is repeated, the template needs A over x minus one, plus B over x minus one squared, plus C over x plus one.
Clear the denominators. Setting x to one gives B equals one-half; setting x to minus one gives C equals minus one-quarter; and comparing the x squared coefficients gives A equals one-quarter.
So the integral is one-quarter log mod x minus one, minus one-half times one over x minus one, minus one-quarter log mod x plus one.
Tidy it up: one-quarter log of the ratio x minus one over x plus one, minus one over two times x minus one, plus C.
<curious>Now the trap that catches everyone, an improper fraction.
We want x cubed over x squared plus one. The numerator's degree, three, is at least the denominator's, so you must divide first: it becomes x minus x over x squared plus one.
Integrate each piece: x squared over two, minus one-half log of x squared plus one, plus C.
That second piece is an f prime over f form, the numerator x is exactly half the derivative of x squared plus one.
The rule: always test the degree first. Skipping the division on an improper fraction is the single most common way this problem goes wrong.
Partial fractions has four reliable traps. Clear them and the method is mechanical.
First and biggest: if the numerator's degree is at least the denominator's, divide first. Forcing partial fractions onto an improper fraction produces wrong constants every time.
Second: a repeated factor, x minus a squared, needs both terms, A over x minus a, and B over x minus a squared. Writing only one is a guaranteed error.
Third: match the numerator to the factor. An irreducible quadratic takes a linear numerator, A x plus B; a linear factor takes just a constant A.
Fourth, a sign check when combining logs: log mod a minus log mod b is log of a over b. Keep track of which factor ends up on top.
The efficiency tip: for distinct linear factors, don't set up a linear system at all, cover-up gives each constant in one substitution.
The board lays out the workflow: improper means divide, then factor, template, solve, integrate.
<whisper>Save coefficient-comparison for repeated or quadratic factors, where cover-up alone can't finish the job.
<curious>Substitution was for a function tangled up with its own derivative. What do we do with a plain product of two unrelated functions?
Think of x times cosine x, or x times e to the x. There's no inner function and its derivative to exploit, so substitution has nothing to grab.
Integration by parts is the tool built exactly for products. It's the reverse of the product rule for differentiation.
The formula trades one integral for another: the integral of u d v equals u v, minus the integral of v d u.

Which factor should be u? Use ILATE, Inverse-trig, Logarithm, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential. The earlier a function sits on that ladder, the better it is as u, because differentiating it simplifies things.
The plan is to differentiate the hard factor u down to something simpler, integrate the easy factor, and hope the new integral is easier than the one you started with.
If your choice makes the new integral harder instead, that's the signal to swap: make the other factor u.
And a few integrals, like e to the x times sine x, cycle back to themselves after two rounds of parts, at which point you solve for the integral algebraically.

board_events.text: Example 1: pick u by ILATE
Evaluate $\int x\cos x\,dx$. Algebraic before Trig, so $u=x$, $dv=\cos x\,dx$; then $du=dx$, $v=\sin x$.

board_events.latex: \int x\cos x\,dx = x\sin x - \int \sin x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x + C

board_events.text: Example 2: the lone ln x trick
Evaluate $\int \ln x\,dx$. Treat it as $\ln x\cdot 1$: $u=\ln x$, $dv=1\,dx$, so $du=\tfrac{1}{x}dx$, $v=x$.

board_events.latex: \int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - \int x\cdot\frac{1}{x}\,dx = x\ln x - x + C

board_events.text: A lone $\ln x$ or $\tan^{-1}x$ pairs with an invisible $\times 1$, then parts applies.
ILATE: differentiate the earlier function — choosing $u=e^x$ over an algebraic term makes it harder.
Example 3: an integral that cycles
Evaluate $I=\int e^x\sin x\,dx$. Parts gives $I = e^x\sin x - \int e^x\cos x\,dx$.
Parts again on the new integral: $\int e^x\cos x\,dx = e^x\cos x + I$.

board_events.latex: I = e^x\sin x - (e^x\cos x + I) \;\Rightarrow\; 2I = e^x(\sin x - \cos x)

board_events.text: Example 4: spot e-to-x times (f + f prime)
Evaluate $\int e^x\left(\tfrac{1}{x}-\tfrac{1}{x^2}\right)dx$. Let $f=\tfrac{1}{x}$, so $f'=-\tfrac{1}{x^2}$ — exactly $e^x[f+f']$.
Recognising $e^x[f+f']$ turns a hard-looking integral into a one-line answer — always check for it.
Integration-by-parts traps
Choose $u$ and $dv$ by ILATE — differentiate the earlier function. The wrong split makes $\int v\,du$ harder.
Sign care: $v=\int\sin x = -\cos x$. Carry that minus through both terms of the formula.
For $\int e^x\sin x$, after two applications the original reappears — solve for it, don't loop forever.
See $e^x$ times a sum? Check whether the second term is the derivative of the first — then use the shortcut.
A lone $\ln x$, $\tan^{-1}x$, or $\sin^{-1}x$? Pair with an invisible $\times 1$ and apply parts.
Test the $f+f'$ pattern before grinding through parts — it converts many hard problems into instant answers.
From a family of curves to one number
An indefinite integral is a family of functions; a definite integral $\int_a^b f\,dx$ is a single number.
Geometrically it's the signed area between $y=f(x)$ and the $x$-axis from $a$ to $b$.

board_events.text: Two definitions agree: a limit of a sum (first principles), and $F(b)-F(a)$ via antiderivatives.
A definite integral has no $+C$ — the constant cancels in $F(b)-F(a)$.
The Fundamental Theorem is the bridge — it makes integration a lookup, not an infinite sum.
Definition, both FTCs, and the structural properties
First FTC in words: differentiating an integral with respect to its upper limit returns the integrand.
A dummy variable: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(t)\,dt$ — the variable's name doesn't matter.
These power-sums are the engine of nearly every limit-of-a-sum evaluation.

segments.text: Let's apply parts cleanly. First, a textbook product.
We want the integral of x cosine x. On the ILATE ladder, Algebraic comes before Trig, so let u be x and d v be cosine x d x. Then d u is d x, and v is sine x.

board_events.text: Example 1: a polynomial
Evaluate $\int_1^2 (3x^2-2x+1)\,dx$. Antiderivative $F(x)=x^3-x^2+x$.
Example 2: limits chosen to collapse logs
Evaluate $\int_1^e \frac{1}{x}\,dx = [\ln x]_1^e = \ln e - \ln 1 = 1$.
Example 3: negative powers
Evaluate $\int_1^2 \left(2x+\frac{3}{x^2}\right)dx$. Antiderivative $F(x)=x^2-\frac{3}{x}$.
Keep the order: upper minus lower, and never write $+C$ on a definite integral.
Example 4: the limit-of-a-sum definition
Evaluate $\int_0^2 (x^2+2x)\,dx$ from first principles. Here $a=0$, $b=2$, $h=\tfrac{2}{n}$, $x_r=\tfrac{2r}{n}$.
As $n\to\infty$, the first term $\to \tfrac{8}{6}\cdot 2 = \tfrac{8}{3}$ and the second $\to 4$.
Check with the FTC: $\left[\tfrac{x^3}{3}+x^2\right]_0^2 = \tfrac{8}{3}+4 = \tfrac{20}{3}$. They agree.
The limit-of-a-sum defines the integral; the FTC is the shortcut. Boards reward showing they agree.
Definite-integral traps
A definite integral is a number — never append $+C$; it cancels in $F(b)-F(a)$.
Keep the FTC order: $F(\text{upper})-F(\text{lower})$. Swapping them flips the sign.
If you ever exchange limits mid-solution, flip the sign to match.
In a limit of a sum, the factor $h=\frac{b-a}{n}$ multiplies the whole sum — dropping it scales the answer wrongly.
Signed area: a dip below the axis subtracts. Total geometric area needs $\int|f|$ — a distinct question.
For first principles, memorise $\sum 1$, $\sum r$, $\sum r^2$ — almost every Board limit reduces to these.
Definite substitution: the limits move too
This fuses substitution with definite integrals. The only new idea is what happens to the limits.
The limits $x=a,b$ are $x$-values; the new integral is in $u$, so convert them: $g(a)$ and $g(b)$.

board_events.text: Change the limits to $u$-values and you never convert back to $x$ — just evaluate in $u$.
Two valid methods: (A) change limits, finish in $u$; (B) keep limits, back-substitute, then evaluate. Never mix.
Watch a non-monotonic $g$ (like $u=x^2$ across $0$) — split the interval first.
The rule and the two-method choice
Method A (preferred): convert the limits to $u$, evaluate in $u$ — no back-substitution.
Method B: keep the $x$-limits, integrate, return to $x$, then apply the original limits.

board_events.text: Example 1: convert both limits
Evaluate $\int_0^1 \frac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx$. Let $u=x^2+1$, $x\,dx=\tfrac{1}{2}du$; limits $0\to 1$, $1\to 2$.
Example 2: a trig substitution
Evaluate $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\cos x\,dx$. Let $u=\sin x$; limits $0\to 0$, $\tfrac{\pi}{2}\to 1$.
Example 3: a log substitution
Evaluate $\int_1^e \frac{\ln x}{x}\,dx$. Let $u=\ln x$; limits $1\to 0$, $e\to 1$: $\int_0^1 u\,du = \tfrac{1}{2}$.
Once the limits are converted, the answer pops out in $u$ — no return to $x$.
Example 4: substitution plus the king property
Evaluate $I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sqrt{\sin x}}{\sqrt{\sin x}+\sqrt{\cos x}}\,dx$. No elementary antiderivative exists.
Apply the king substitution $x\to\tfrac{\pi}{2}-x$, which swaps $\sin\leftrightarrow\cos$ but keeps the limits.
Add the two expressions for $I$: the denominators match, so the numerators sum to the whole.
The king substitution is a limit-preserving change of variable — the cleanest link to the properties.
When no antiderivative exists, a limit-preserving substitution can still deliver a clean number.
Definite-substitution traps
Switched to $u$? The limits must become $g(a)$ and $g(b)$. Keeping old $x$-limits is the top error.
Never mix methods: either change the limits, or back-substitute — doing both corrupts the bounds.
The $du$ scaling still applies to the limits-changed integral: e.g. the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ from $x\,dx=\tfrac{1}{2}du$.
Non-monotonic $g$ (e.g. $u=x^2$ across $0$)? Split the interval before substituting.
Prefer Method A — changing the limits removes the back-substitution step and a whole class of errors.
Write the new $u$-limits right next to the integral sign so you can't forget them.
Compute without an antiderivative
Properties let you evaluate an integral by exploiting symmetry — no antiderivative required.
A definite integral is an accumulated area; area doesn't care which way you sweep or where the origin sits.

segments.text: Let's practise Method A: change the limits, then never look back at x.
We want the integral from zero to one of x over x squared plus one. Let u be x squared plus one, so x d x is one-half d u. Convert the limits: x zero gives u one, x one gives u two.
The integral becomes one-half, times the integral from one to two of d u over u, which is one-half log u from one to two, that's one-half log two.
Next, a trig substitution, and watch how neatly the limits fall.
We want the integral from zero to pi over two of sine x cosine x. Let u be sine x. Convert: x zero gives u zero, and x pi over two gives u one.
The integral becomes the integral from zero to one of u d u, which is u squared over two, from zero to one, simply one-half.
One more, with a logarithm.
We want the integral from one to e of log x over x. Let u be log x. Convert: x one gives u zero, x e gives u one. Again it's the integral of u from zero to one, which is one-half.

board_events.text: Example 1: split a modulus with additivity
Evaluate $\int_0^4 |x-2|\,dx$. Split at $x=2$: $|x-2|=2-x$ for $x<2$, $x-2$ for $x>2$.
Example 2: parity kills terms
Evaluate $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(x^2\sin x + x\cos x + 4)\,dx$ mentally, using symmetric limits.
Parity: $x^2\sin x$ is odd (even$\times$odd), $x\cos x$ is odd, $4$ is even — only the constant survives.
Never integrate $x^2\sin x$ or $x\cos x$ here — symmetry deletes them before you start.
Symmetric limits? Split into even and odd parts; every odd term is instantly zero.
Example 3: king peels off the x
Evaluate $I=\int_0^{\pi} x\sin^3 x\,dx$. Apply king with $x\to\pi-x$; since $\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x$, only the $x$ changes.
So $2I = \pi\int_0^{\pi}\sin^3 x\,dx$, and $\int_0^{\pi}\sin^3 x\,dx = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^3 x\,dx = 2\cdot\tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{4}{3}$.
Example 4: the periodic property
Evaluate $\int_0^{10\pi}|\sin x|\,dx$. Since $|\sin x|$ has period $\pi$, there are $10$ full periods.
Use the modulus period $\pi$; pairing period $2\pi$ with a dropped modulus wrongly gives $0$.
Property traps and the recognition reflex
Even/odd needs limits $[-a,a]$. On $[0,2]$ or $[1,3]$, parity tells you nothing.
King replaces $x$ by $a+b-x$ — not simply $a-x$ unless the lower limit is $0$.
A modulus or greatest-integer must be split where the inside changes sign — never integrated as one formula.
For $|\sin x|,|\cos x|$ the period is $\pi$. Pairing period $2\pi$ with a dropped modulus gives a wrong $0$.
After the king 'add' trick, $2I=$ (easy) — divide by two. Skipping this doubles the answer.
Read the limits first, integrand second — most 'hard' property problems are pattern recognition.

segments.text: Let's put the toolkit to work. First, a modulus, handled by splitting.
We want the integral from zero to four of the absolute value of x minus two. The expression inside changes sign at x equals two, so split there.
For x below two, the absolute value is two minus x; above two, it's x minus two. Each piece is a small triangle of area two, so the total is two plus two, which is four.
<excited>Now a problem you can do almost entirely in your head, thanks to symmetry.
We want the integral from minus pi over two to pi over two of x squared sine x, plus x cosine x, plus four. The limits are symmetric, so check the parity of each term.
x squared sine x is even times odd, so it's odd and vanishes. x cosine x is odd times even, also odd and vanishes. Only the constant four, which is even, survives.
So the whole thing reduces to the integral of four across the symmetric interval, which is four times the width pi, that's four pi.
The takeaway: never grind through x squared sine x or x cosine x here. Symmetry deletes both before you write a single step.
Whenever the limits are symmetric, split the integrand into even and odd parts, and every odd term is instantly zero.
Now the king property, used to peel an awkward x off a trig function.

We want capital I, the integral from zero to pi of x times sine cubed x. Apply king: replace x with pi minus x. Since sine of pi minus x is just sine x, the sine cubed is untouched, only the lone x becomes pi minus x.
So I equals the integral of pi minus x, times sine cubed x. Expanding, that's pi times the integral of sine cubed, minus I itself.

Move the I over: two I equals pi times the integral of sine cubed x from zero to pi. And sine cubed is symmetric about pi over two, so that integral is twice the integral from zero to pi over two, which is two times two-thirds, giving four-thirds.
So two I equals pi times four-thirds, and I is two pi over three. The king folded the awkward x into a constant pi and the integral solved itself.
<curious>Now the periodic property, and a modulus trap to avoid.

We want the integral from zero to ten pi of the absolute value of sine x. The key is the period: the modulus folds the negative humps up, so the absolute value of sine x has period pi. That means ten full periods on this interval.
So it's ten times the integral from zero to pi of the absolute value of sine x, and on zero to pi, sine is non-negative, so that's just ten times the integral of sine x.
The integral of sine x from zero to pi is minus cosine, evaluated, giving one plus one, which is two. So the whole thing is ten times two, which is twenty.
The trap: use the modulus period pi. Students who write period two pi and then forget the modulus let the second hump cancel the first, and wrongly get zero.
The properties are powerful, but they punish a few specific slips. Let's name them.
First: even-odd cancellation needs symmetric limits, minus a to a. On zero to two, or one to three, parity tells you nothing, a very common reflex error.

Second: king replaces x by the sum of the limits minus x, that's a plus b minus x. It's only a minus x when the lower limit happens to be zero. Using the wrong replacement silently wrecks the cancellation.
Third: a modulus or greatest-integer must be split at the points where the inside changes sign. Integrating it as a single formula is wrong.
Fourth: for the absolute value of sine or cosine, the period is pi, not two pi. Pairing period two pi with a dropped modulus is the classic double-error that returns zero.
Fifth: after the king add-trick gives you two I equals something easy, divide by two. Skipping that step doubles every king answer.
The board captures the whole decision tree: symmetric means parity, zero to a with trig means king, modulus means split, whole periods means collapse.
<whisper>The master habit: read the limits first, the integrand second. Ninety percent of hard property problems are pattern recognition, the algebra is the easy part.

We want the integral from zero to four of the absolute value of x minus two. The expression inside changes sign at x equals two, so split there.

<excited>Now a problem you can do almost entirely in your head, thanks to symmetry.
We want the integral from minus pi over two to pi over two of x squared sine x, plus x cosine x, plus four. The limits are symmetric, so check the parity of each term.

sections.title: Trig examples: odd powers and Walli's formula & related topics

board_events.text: Example 3: an odd power, peel and substitute
Evaluate $\int \sin^3 x\cos^2 x\,dx$. Peel one $\sin x$: $\sin^3 x = (1-\cos^2 x)\sin x$.
Let $u=\cos x$, $du=-\sin x\,dx$.
Example 4: Walli's formula
Evaluate $\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^6 x\cos^2 x\,dx$. Here $n=6$, $m=2$, both even, so the $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ branch applies.
Walli collapses a brutal expansion into one double-factorial fraction — priceless when time is short.
The formula and its two golden results

board_events.latex: \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du \qquad \int u\,v'\,dx = uv - \int u'\,v\,dx

board_events.text: ILATE picks u: Inverse-trig, Logarithm, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential — earlier means differentiate it.

board_events.latex: \int e^{ax}\sin bx\,dx = \frac{e^{ax}(a\sin bx - b\cos bx)}{a^2+b^2} + C
\int e^{ax}\cos bx\,dx = \frac{e^{ax}(a\cos bx + b\sin bx)}{a^2+b^2} + C

board_events.text: Derivation: integrate the product rule $(uv)'=u'v+uv'$ and rearrange for $\int uv'\,dx$.
See $e^x$ times a sum? Check if the second term is the derivative of the first — then jump to $e^x f(x)$.
Integrals — quick recall
Always add $+C$ for indefinite integrals; a definite integral is a number with no $+C$.
'Co goes positive': $\int\cos = +\sin$; the plain sine integral carries the minus.
'One over x is the lonely log': $\frac{1}{x}$ never obeys the power rule — it integrates to $\ln|x|$.
Substitution reflex: numerator = derivative of denominator $\Rightarrow$ a log. 'Convert there, convert back.'
Special forms: 'Plus is arctan, minus is log'; 'arcsin has no $\tfrac{1}{a}$.'
Partial fractions: 'Improper? Divide before you decide'; 'repeated factor gives repeated terms.'
Parts: ILATE picks $u$; '$e^x(f+f')=e^x f$'; king — 'solve for $I$, then halve.'
Definite: 'upper minus lower, no C'; 'odd dies on a mirror'; 'modulus halves the period.'

segments.text: Odd powers get a different treatment, peel and substitute.
We want the integral of sine cubed x cosine squared x. Since the sine power is odd, peel off one sine x and convert the rest: sine cubed becomes one minus cosine squared, times sine x.
Now let u be cosine x, so d u is minus sine x d x, and that spare sine x is exactly what we need.
The integral becomes minus the integral of one minus u squared, times u squared, d u, that is minus u cubed over three, minus u to the fifth over five, with the sign worked through.
Back-substitute u equals cosine x, and after tidying signs the answer is cosine to the fifth x over five, minus cosine cubed x over three, plus C.
<excited>Now a definite integral where Walli's formula turns a nightmare into one line.
We want the integral from zero to pi over two of sine to the sixth x, cosine squared x. Here n is six and m is two, both even, so the pi-over-two branch of Walli applies.

Plug in the double-factorials: five double-factorial times one double-factorial, over eight double-factorial, times pi over two. That's fifteen over three hundred eighty-four, times pi over two, which simplifies to five pi over two hundred fifty-six.
See what Walli bought us: it collapsed a brutal expansion into a single double-factorial fraction. When the clock is running, that's priceless.

Rule zero: indefinite integrals hamesha plus C lete hain; definite integral ek number hai, bilkul koi plus C nahi.
Trig signs ke liye yaad rakho co goes positive, cosine integrate hokar plus sine, aur plain sine integral wo hai jo minus rakhta hai.
One over x is the lonely log, yah kabhi power rule nahin maanta; hamesha log mod x mein integrate hota hai.
Substitution reflex: agar numerator denominator ka derivative hai, answer ek log hai. aur convert there, convert back, answer kabhi u mein mat chhodo.
Special forms ke liye: plus is arctan, minus is log, aur yaad rakho, arcsine form mein koi one-over-a nahi.
Partial fractions ke liye: improper? Divide before you decide. aur repeated factor matlab template mein repeated terms.
Parts ke liye: ILATE u chunta hai; e to the x times f plus f-prime simatkar e to the x times f; aur king trick ke baad, solve for I, phir halve karo.
Definite integrals ke liye: upper minus lower, no C; odd dies on a mirror; aur modulus period ko aadha karta hai. inhen saath le jao, aur integration recognition ban jaati hai.

chunk_timeline.text: Odd powers ka ilaaj alag hai, peel karo aur substitute karo.
humein integral chahiye sine cube x cosine square x ka. chuki sine ki power odd hai, ek sine x chhilo aur baaki ko badlo: sine cube banta hai one minus cosine square, times sine x.
ab maan lo u hai cosine x, to d u hai minus sine x d x, aur wo bacha hua sine x theek wahi hai jo chahiye.
Integral ban jata hai minus integral of one minus u square, times u square, d u, yaani minus u cube bata three, minus u to the fifth bata five, sign sambhalte hue.
wapas rakho u barabar cosine x, aur signs theek karne par answer hai cosine to the fifth x bata five, minus cosine cube x bata three, plus C.
ab ek definite integral jahan Walli's formula ek nightmare ko ek line bana deta hai.
humein integral chahiye zero to pi over two, sine to the sixth x, cosine square x ka. yahaan n hai six aur m hai two, dono even, to Walli ka pi-over-two branch lagta hai.

Double-factorials rakho: five double-factorial times one double-factorial, bata eight double-factorial, times pi over two. Yah hai fifteen bata three hundred eighty-four, times pi over two, jo simatkar banta hai five pi bata two hundred fifty-six.
dekho Walli ne kya diya: ek brutal expansion ko ek akele double-factorial fraction mein sikod diya. jab ghadi chal rahi ho, yah anmol hai.
yah raha formula aur vo do high-value results jo mushkil problems ko one-liner bana dete hain.
Core formula: integral of u d v barabar u v minus integral of v d u. Yaane u ko differentiate karo, v prime ko integrate karo, aur bacha hua integral ghatao.
u chunne ke liye ILATE istemal karo, Inverse-trig, Logarithm, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential. Is list mein jo pehle aaye, usi ko differentiate karo.
Golden shortcut: integral of e to the x times f plus f prime bas e to the x times f, plus C hai.
yaad rakhne layak do cycling results: integral of e to the a x sine b x hai e to the a x, times a sine b x minus b cosine b x, bata a square plus b square.
aur iska partner: integral of e to the a x cosine b x hai e to the a x, times a cosine b x plus b sine b x, bata a square plus b square.
mukhya formula kahaan se aata hai? bas product rule integrate karo, u v prime plus u prime v, aur u v prime ke integral ko alag karne ke liye rearrange karo.
